Everything you need to pass telc B1.

You're in a B1.1 course now, and your exam is in the first week of December, about 12 weeks away. This guide is your single source: all the grammar explained simply, the vocabulary theme by theme with memory tricks, ready-made letters for the writing test, full dialogues for the speaking test, and a 12-week plan that runs next to your course and then trains you for the exam. Work through it and walk in prepared.

Exam

The exam, part by part

READ THIS FIRST

Know every task, every point and every rule before you walk in. No surprises = calm brain = more points.

📝 The written exam — 225 points, 9 tasks

The written exam takes about 2½ hours of work plus a 20-minute break. It always runs in this order. All numbers below come from the official telc materials.

TaskWhat you getPointsStrategy in one line
Lesen 1
global		5 short texts + 10 headlines: match each text to its headline25
(5 × 5)		Read for the main idea, not every word.
Lesen 2
detail		1 long newspaper text + 5 multiple-choice questions (a/b/c)25
(5 × 5)		The questions follow the text order.
Lesen 3
selective		10 situations + 12 small ads: find the ad that fits each situation25
(10 × 2,5)		Check date, place, price. No fit? Mark x.
Sprachbausteine 1A letter with 10 gaps, 3 options per gap — grammar15
(10 × 1,5)		Connectors, prepositions, pronouns, verb forms.
Sprachbausteine 2A letter with 10 gaps, choose from 15 words — vocabulary15
(10 × 1,5)		Fixed word pairs. Fill the easy gaps first.
Hören 1
global		5 short texts, richtig/falsch — plays ONCE25
(5 × 5)		Read all 5 statements before the audio starts.
Hören 2
detail		1 long conversation/interview, 10 richtig/falsch — plays twice25
(10 × 2,5)		1st listen: answer. 2nd listen: check.
Hören 3
selective		5 announcements, richtig/falsch — plays twice25
(5 × 5)		Hunt for numbers, times, prices, places.
Brief
(writing)		1 semi-formal letter/e-mail answering 4 guiding points, 30 min45Cover all 4 points — that is most of the marks.
The clock, exactly: ① Reading + Sprachbausteine share one 90-minute block — you decide how to split it. ② 20-minute break. ③ Listening, about 30 minutes — the audio controls the speed, not you. ④ The letter is its own separate 30-minute block at the end.
Common mistake: people think they must "save" reading time for the letter. No! The letter has its own 30 minutes — you can never borrow time between blocks. So use the full 90 minutes for reading + gaps, and keep about 10 of those minutes to copy your answers onto the answer sheet (der Antwortbogen — the official sheet the machine reads; only answers on it count).

🗣️ The oral exam — 75 points, 3 parts, usually done in pairs

You normally speak with another candidate in front of two examiners (only if the number of candidates is odd is it done solo, with an examiner as your partner). The talk itself lasts at most 15 minutes per pair. Before it, you get 20 minutes of preparation time with the task sheets — you may write short notes, but in the exam you should talk, not read aloud.

PartWhat happensTime · Points
Teil 1
Kontaktaufnahme		"Making contact": you introduce yourselves and ask each other simple personal questions (job, family, hobbies, languages).3–4 min · 15
Teil 2
Gespräch über ein Thema		"Conversation about a topic": each of you gets short info on a topic; you report it, give your opinion and experience, and react to your partner.5–6 min · 30
Teil 3
Gemeinsam etwas planen		"Planning something together" (official name: Gemeinsam eine Aufgabe lösen — solving a task together): suggest, agree, disagree politely, decide together.5–6 min · 30

How the 75 points are scored

Both examiners score you separately during the talk, then agree on a mark after you leave the room. Each part is rated on the same four things:

  • Ausdrucksfähigkeit — expression: can you say what you mean, with enough words?
  • Aufgabenbewältigung — doing the task: did you really discuss / plan / react to your partner?
  • Formale Richtigkeit — accuracy: grammar and sentence building.
  • Aussprache und Intonation — pronunciation and melody: easy to understand?
Good news: at B1 level, examiners expect mistakes. A wrong article costs almost nothing. Silence, or ignoring your partner, costs a lot. Keep talking, keep reacting — that is what "Aufgabenbewältigung" rewards.

✅ Pass rules — super simple

  • Written exam: 225 points possible → you need 135 (that is 60%).
  • Oral exam: 75 points possible → you need 45 (also 60%).
  • You must reach 60% in both parts. A great written score cannot rescue a failed oral, and the other way round.
  • Failed (or missed) only ONE part? You may repeat just that part — in the same calendar year or the next one. The part you passed stays valid.
  • The whole exam can be repeated as often as you want.
Memory trickThink "60 + 60": sixty percent written and sixty percent oral. Two separate doors — you must open both.

Your grade (only if you passed both parts)

Add your written + oral points together (maximum 300):

GradeMeaningTotal points
sehr gutvery good270–300
gutgood240–269,5
befriedigendsatisfactory210–239,5
ausreichendsufficient (pass)180–209,5
For almost every purpose (job, visa, citizenship, university application) only "bestanden" (passed) matters, not the grade. Aim for solid 60–70% everywhere — don't chase perfection.

📖 Leseverstehen — how to beat each reading task

Teil 1 (headlines): read the text FIRST

Read one short text, say its main idea to yourself in your own words, and only then look for the headline that says the same idea. There are 10 headlines for 5 texts, so 5 headlines are traps.

The word trap: a wrong headline often repeats one word from the text. Same word ≠ same meaning. Match the idea, never a single word.

Teil 2 (long text): questions first, in order

Read the 5 questions before the text. The questions follow the text from top to bottom, so once you have found the answer to question 2, the answer to question 3 comes later in the text. Answer only from what the text says — not from your own knowledge or opinion.

Teil 3 (ads): every condition must fit

Underline the 2–3 conditions in each situation (what? when? how much?), then scan the 12 ads. An ad is only correct if all conditions fit. Each ad can be used only once — and if no ad fits a situation, you mark x on the answer sheet.

Situation: Sie suchen eine 2-Zimmer-Wohnung mit Balkon für maximal 600 Euro.Situation: You are looking for a 2-room flat with a balcony for a maximum of 600 euros.
Anzeige: Schöne 2-Zimmer-Wohnung mit Balkon, 650 Euro.Ad: Nice 2-room flat with balcony, 650 euros.
Balcony ✓, 2 rooms ✓ — but 650 > 600, so this ad is wrong. One broken condition kills the whole match. This is exactly how telc builds its traps.

Suggested time budget (inside the 90-minute block)

  • Lesen 1 — about 12 minutes
  • Lesen 2 — about 20 minutes
  • Lesen 3 — about 20 minutes
  • Sprachbausteine 1 + 2 — about 25 minutes
  • Copy answers to the Antwortbogen + final check — about 13 minutes

🧩 Sprachbausteine — 30 fast points if you know the patterns

Teil 1 tests grammar (10 gaps, 3 options each)

  • Connectors — weil vs. denn vs. deshalb vs. obwohl: the word order around the gap tells you the answer.
  • Prepositions — an, auf, für, mit, bei, von… mostly the fixed verb + preposition pairs.
  • Verb forms — würde/könnte/hätte, Perfekt forms, reflexive pronouns (mich, dich, sich).
  • Pronouns & articles — der/dem/den, relative pronouns, Ihnen vs. Sie.

Teil 2 tests vocabulary (10 gaps, choose from 15 words)

  • Fixed expressions and word partners: Vielen Dank für…, Ich freue mich auf…, typical letter phrases.
  • 15 words for 10 gaps → 5 words are never used. Fill the easy gaps first; every filled gap removes a word and makes the hard gaps easier.
  • Check what word type the gap needs: after "der/die/das" a noun, before a noun maybe an adjective, in position 2 a verb.
Method for every gap: read the whole sentence (often also the sentence before), decide what type of word is missing, then test each option quietly "by ear". Never answer a gap in isolation.
There is no penalty for wrong answers — so never, ever leave a gap empty. A blind guess is free points waiting to happen.
✍️ Try it — a mini Sprachbausteine round 4 gaps

Fill the gaps in this short reply to a course office:

Liebe Frau Berg,

vielen Dank (1) ___ Ihre E-Mail. Ich kann leider nicht am Kurs teilnehmen, (2) ___ ich nächste Woche arbeiten muss. Ich würde mich freuen, (3) ___ Sie mir einen anderen Termin anbieten könnten. Ich warte (4) ___ Ihre Antwort.

Viele Grüße
Sadman

  • (1) a) für   b) über   c) um
  • (2) a) denn   b) deshalb   c) weil
  • (3) a) dass   b) wenn   c) ob
  • (4) a) an   b) auf   c) für

Answers — and why

GapAnswerWhy
1a) fürFixed pair: danken für — you always thank FOR something.
2c) weilThe verb "muss" sits at the end of the clause → that is "weil" word order. With "denn" the verb would come earlier: "…, denn ich muss arbeiten."
3b) wenn"I would be happy IF you could…" — "dass" (= that) and "ob" (= whether) don't fit the meaning here.
4b) aufFixed pair: warten auf + Akkusativ (the case for the thing the action points at).
Vielen Dank für Ihre E-Mail.Thank you very much for your e-mail.
Ich kann leider nicht am Kurs teilnehmen, weil ich nächste Woche arbeiten muss.Unfortunately I can't take part in the course, because I have to work next week.
Ich würde mich freuen, wenn Sie mir einen anderen Termin anbieten könnten.I would be happy if you could offer me another date.
Ich warte auf Ihre Antwort.I am waiting for your reply.

🎧 Hörverstehen — listening without panic

The golden rule: read the statements BEFORE the audio

The recording always gives you time to read the statements first — use every second of it. Underline the key word in each statement. While listening, you only check: does the audio say this, yes or no?

Teil 1 plays only ONCE. This is the hardest moment of the whole exam — there is no second chance. Train this part more than any other: full focus for those few minutes, phone away, one listen only when you practise.

Teil 2 (long conversation, plays twice)

The 10 statements follow the conversation in order. First listen: answer everything you can. Second listen: check and fix. If you missed one, mark a guess and let it go — richtig/falsch means even a blind guess wins half the time.

Teil 3 (announcements, plays twice): hunt the numbers

Announcements at stations, on answering machines, on the radio. The answer almost always hides in a number, time, price, date or platform — write these down the moment you hear them.

Der Zug nach Hamburg fährt heute um 14:30 Uhr von Gleis 7.The train to Hamburg leaves today at 2:30 pm from platform 7.
Never chase a lost answer. If you miss item 47, guess it and jump to item 48. Chasing one answer into the next text is how people lose three points instead of one.

🎒 Exam day — your checklist

Pack the bag the evening before. Tap each item to tick it off:

  • Personalausweis or passport — the SAME ID you used when you registered
  • Registration confirmation / invitation letter from the exam centre
  • Check the address, room and travel route one day before
  • Arrive 30 minutes early — late arrivals can be refused
  • Two pens (blue or black) + a pencil for notes
  • Water bottle and a small snack for the 20-minute break
  • Phone switched OFF and in your bag — smartwatches count as phones
  • No dictionary, no notes, no vocabulary lists on the desk
  • Glasses or hearing aid if you need them
  • On the way there: listen to easy German audio to warm up your ears
  • The night before: sleep well, review only old notes — nothing new
  • During the exam: watch the clock and never leave any answer empty
Last thought before the door: you do not need 100%. You need 60% — and you are allowed to make mistakes in every single part and still pass. Breathe, read the task, collect the easy points first. Viel Erfolg! (Good luck!)
Plan

Your plan: B1.1 course → telc B1 in early December

START HERE

12 weeks. Weeks 1–8 run next to your B1.1 course (it ends on 4 November). Weeks 9–12 are pure exam training. On course days, 30–60 minutes is enough (your course homework comes first). Weekends are longer. Tired today? Read only two cards: "I didn't understand anything" and this weekend. The rest can wait until Monday.

🤝 The honest answer: "Will I pass if I do all this?"

Nobody can promise you 100%. Not this guide, not your teacher, not any book. Be careful with anyone who promises that. Here is what is true:

  • You need 60%, not perfection. 135 of 225 points in the written exam and 45 of 75 in the speaking exam. Mistakes are expected at B1, and you can make mistakes in every part and still pass.
  • The two parts are separate. If you pass one and fail the other, you keep the part you passed and repeat only the other one (details in the exam section).
  • This guide covers what can be learned from a page: all the B1 grammar, the vocabulary themes, every exam task, ready-made letters and speaking scripts, and 373 practice questions.
  • It cannot train your ears or your mouth. Listening needs real audio, and speaking needs real conversations. That's why the plan has listening every day and a speaking partner every week. Those minutes matter more than any extra page you read.
The timeline, honestly: B1.1 is only the first half of B1, and the exam tests all of B1. So taking it after B1.1 plus 4 weeks of training is ambitious but possible. In the exam, good strategy and ready-made phrases win many points, and you only need 60%. All of that can be trained. You don't have to decide today. After two classes, nobody can know. Instead, you do a full practice test at the checkpoint, and the score tells you what to do:
Your practice-test score (written part)What it meansWhat to do
about 55% or moreYou are on track.Keep the December exam. The 4 training weeks will add points.
about 45–55%Close. Possible with daily work.Keep December only if you can study every day and your teacher agrees. Put extra time into the letter (45 points), because learned phrases win points there fastest.
clearly under 45%Very hard to close in 4 weeks.Talk to your teacher. Doing B1.2 too and taking the exam in January or February is not a failure. It's the normal route, and nothing you learned is lost. Already registered? Ask the exam centre if you can move to a later date.

How to count: check reading, Sprachbausteine and listening with the answer key. The points for each question are in the exam section table. You can't mark your own letter well, so ask your teacher to mark it. Speaking is scored separately (45 of 75), so also do all 3 speaking parts with your partner before you decide. These percentages are a rough guide from experience, not an official telc rule.

When is the checkpoint? Normally in week 7 (26 Oct – 1 Nov). But your decision must come before your registration deadline, and deadlines are often several weeks before the exam, so for early December it may already be in October. If your deadline is earlier than week 7, do the checkpoint test on the weekend before your deadline.
What makes the biggest difference is not talent. It's doing a little every single day: 10 words, 15–20 minutes of listening, speaking out loud, and a few full practice tests with a clock. Follow the plan and you give yourself a real chance.

😵 "I didn't understand anything in the first classes." That's normal.

A new level always starts like this. The teacher speaks faster, talks about grammar in German, and uses words like Partizip or Nebensatz. You also saw that the other students didn't understand either. That shows that a big part of the problem is the jump to a new level, not you. Most of the gap is forgotten basics and grammar words. If your last course was A2.1, some A2 rules are not forgotten but new for you. That's a known gap, and the A2 lessons in the review cover it. All of this can be fixed, step by step:

  1. In class: take a photo of the board (you already do this!).
  2. The same evening: press 🔎 Search and type what's on the board, like Präteritum, gearbeitet or als. Read the card that comes up.
  3. Grammar word you don't know? Look it up in the glossary, which gives German term → plain English.
  4. An old rule you forgot, or never learned? Do its lesson in the A1 → A2 review, then the quick check at the end.
  5. New verbs? Type each one into the verb lookup and say the 3 forms out loud: arbeiten – arbeitete – hat gearbeitet.
SAY THIS IN CLASS — IT'S NORMAL AND POLITE
  • Können Sie das bitte noch einmal erklären? — Could you please explain that again?
  • Können Sie bitte langsamer sprechen? — Could you please speak more slowly?
  • Was bedeutet „Partizip“? — What does "Partizip" mean?
  • Können Sie das bitte an die Tafel schreiben? — Could you please write that on the board?
  • Viele von uns haben das nicht verstanden. Können wir noch ein Beispiel machen? — Many of us didn't understand that. Can we do another example?
Still lost after 3–4 weeks? Talk to your teacher after class: „Ich komme im Kurs nicht mit. Was empfehlen Sie mir?“ (I can't keep up in the course. What do you recommend?) Repeating B1.1 or moving to a slower course is common, and it is not a failure. Keep going to class. You don't need to understand every word. Try to understand the example on the board.
Team up. The others are just as lost, which makes them perfect study partners. Ask: „Wollen wir zusammen lernen?“ (Shall we study together?) From week 2, meet once a week for an hour and practise speaking. No partner in class? Ask at your Volkshochschule or library for a free Sprachcafé (conversation café), or look for a tandem partner. In the exam you speak with a partner you may not know, so practising with different people helps.

🚀 This weekend (11–13 September): small steps

Week 1 starts on Monday. Before that, only this:

  • Tonight (Friday, 10 minutes): do the 36-question check and write down the lesson numbers you got wrong. Those lessons go first. Then stop and rest.
  • Saturday (about 1 hour): open your board photos from the first two classes. For each photo, do the 5 steps from the card above, starting with the verbs. You don't need to understand everything, only a bit more than in class.
  • Sunday: write to your exam centre (the school where you want to take the exam, often a Volkshochschule or a language school). Ask about the December dates, the registration deadline, the fee, and what happens if you need to move or cancel. Dates can fill up, registration usually closes several weeks before the exam, and after the deadline you may lose part or all of the fee. Write the deadline in your calendar. Make sure the exam is called telc Deutsch B1 (also called "Zertifikat Deutsch"), because that is the exam this guide is built for. You can copy the email below.
  • Also on Sunday: download the official telc Deutsch B1 Übungstest (free PDF + MP3 from telc.net) for week 4. Then tap set date at the top of this page and enter your exam date for the countdown. A guess is fine for now.
YOUR EMAIL TO THE EXAM CENTRE — COPY IT
  • Guten Tag, — Hello,
  • ich möchte im Dezember die Prüfung „telc Deutsch B1“ machen. — I would like to take the "telc Deutsch B1" exam in December.
  • Wann sind die Termine im Dezember? — When are the dates in December?
  • Bis wann muss ich mich anmelden, und wie viel kostet die Prüfung? — By when do I have to register, and how much does the exam cost?
  • Kann ich den Termin später verschieben oder absagen? — Can I move or cancel the date later?
  • Vielen Dank für Ihre Antwort! — Thank you very much for your answer!
  • Mit freundlichen Grüßen + your name — Kind regards + your name
Also ask your teacher: many schools run the exam themselves and offer a short exam-prep course (Prüfungsvorbereitung) in November. That would be perfect for weeks 9–12. If an office (for example the Jobcenter) pays for your course, ask whether it also pays for the exam.

⏰ Your daily routine

Same shape every day. You don't have to decide what to do, so it's easier to start.

BlockCourse day (≈ 45–60 min, after homework)Busy day (30 min minimum)Weekend (≈ 2 hours, one day)
After class + Basics20 min: the 5 steps from the card above, for what your class did today. Time left? Do the next item from this week's Basics list.10 min: search today's board topic and read the card45 min: the Basics lessons and cards you didn't finish this week + one practice gym drill
Vocabulary15 min: 10 new words as short sentences + review yesterday's + review the same day last week10 min: review yesterday's words15 min: review the whole week

Speaking5–10 min: tell your phone about your day in the past tense, out loud, and record it—30 min with your speaking partner (from week 2)
Writing (from week 3)——30 min: one letter with a timer
Heute habe ich im Kurs das Präteritum gelernt. Am Abend habe ich zwanzig Minuten Deutsch gehört.Today I learned the Präteritum in class. In the evening I listened to German for twenty minutes.This is your speaking habit: 3–6 sentences about today, out loud.
Try to never have a zero day. A short day still counts. Missed a day anyway? Don't do double the next day. Just do the normal plan and continue. From week 9, when the course is over, plan about 2 hours a day (a practice-test day takes about 3 hours).
🧠 How to learn words so they stick chunks + spaced repetition

Never learn a word alone. Learn it inside a short sentence (a "chunk"). A chunk stores the article, the case and the preposition for free, and it gives you something ready to say.

Not just „der Termin“, but: Ich habe einen Termin beim Arzt.Not just "the appointment", but: I have an appointment at the doctor's.

Repeat at growing distances (spaced repetition): every day you learn 10 new chunks, review yesterday's, and review the ones from the same day last week. Repeating at growing distances is what moves words into long-term memory.

📚 Weeks 1–8: next to your B1.1 course

Every week has the same 4 parts. Course means the after-class routine for whatever your class did. Basics means the old rules and verb forms, in the order that helps your course most. Words means one vocabulary theme. Skills means listening, writing and speaking. Lessons you got wrong in the 36-question check always go first. You will not finish every week, and that's OK. Take what's left into the next week, but don't drop the listening to catch up. Need one verb in every tense and person? Card 10 is your reference table at any time.

Week 1 (14–20 Sep): Perfekt, because your class uses it right now
  • Basics: Verb forms cards 1, 2, 3 (the 3 forms, how to build the Partizip II, hat or ist), then practice gym drills 1–3 (card 13). Review lessons 13 and 14 (Perfekt 1 and 2), then 1 and 2.
  • Words: Words 1: people and family.
  • Skills: listening every day: Nicos Weg (3–4 short episodes) and Nachrichtenleicht.
  • Goal: say the 10 verbs from your teacher's whiteboard (in card 2) with their 3 forms and hat or ist, without looking.
Week 2 (21–27 Sep): the past: Perfekt, Präteritum, haben and sein
  • Basics: cards 4, 6, 7, 9 (which past, haben, sein, how to build the Präteritum), then practice gym drills 4 and 7. Lessons 15 (the short past), 3, 4, 5.
  • Words: Words 1: feelings and relationships.
  • Skills: find your speaking partner and meet once this week.
  • Goal: tell your weekend out loud in 6 sentences (Perfekt + war / hatte / musste).
Week 3 (28 Sep – 4 Oct): werden, modal verbs, now-forms + your first letter
  • Basics: cards 5, 8, 11, 12, then practice gym drills 5 and 6. Lessons 9 (modal verbs), 8, 6, 7, 10.
  • Words: Words 2: home, food, shopping.
  • Skills: learn the letter skeleton in Writing and copy one model letter by hand.
  • Goal: 10 of 12 or better in practice gym drill 6 (modal verbs).
Week 4 (5–11 Oct): prepositions and cases + practice test 1
  • Basics: lessons 11, 12, 16, 17, 18 (imperative, time words, Dativ, prepositions, Wo or Wohin).
  • Words: Words 3: health, daily life, environment.
  • Practice test 1: reading + Sprachbausteine (90 min) and listening (about 30 min) from the official Übungstest. Write your score in your notebook. A low score now is normal, because you haven't learned the exam tricks yet. Show the score to your teacher and ask: „Glauben Sie, dass ich die B1-Prüfung im Dezember schaffen kann?“ (Do you think I can pass the B1 exam in December?)
  • Skills: 1 letter, copied and changed a little.
  • Goal: know your starting score and your 2 weakest parts.
Week 5 (12–18 Oct): building sentences
  • Basics: lessons 19–24 (reflexive verbs, weil/dass/wenn, indirect questions, connectors, comparing, adjective endings).
  • Words: Words 4: work, school, offices.
  • Skills: for speaking part 1, write your 90-second self-introduction, record it, and learn 5 questions to ask your partner (part 1 is a conversation, not a speech). Write 1 letter without looking (40 min). Listening: add the slowly spoken news (see the listening list).
  • Goal: 10 sentences with weil / dass / wenn / obwohl, verb at the end.
Week 6 (19–25 Oct): would-forms, verbs with prepositions, numbers, questions
  • Basics: lessons 25–30.
  • Words: finish Words 4, start Words 5: travel, city.
  • Skills: speaking part 2 with your partner: 2 topic mini-talks. 1 letter in 35 minutes.
  • Goal: you know your exact registration deadline. If it is in October, do practice test 2 this weekend or the weekend before the deadline, decide, and register in time.
Week 7 (26 Oct – 1 Nov): checkpoint week
  • Basics: lessons 31–36.
  • Practice test 2 (if you haven't done it before your deadline): a full written test you have never seen, on a weekend, with the exact exam clock: reading + Sprachbausteine 90 min, 20 min break, listening, letter 30 min. No dictionary, no phone, no pausing the audio. Ask your teacher to mark the letter. Then use the checkpoint table and decide.
  • Words: Words 5.
  • Skills: speaking part 3 (planning something together) with your partner.
  • Goal: your decision is made. Either you're registered for December, or you do B1.2 first. If you choose B1.2, keep the same daily routine and use weeks 9–12 as the last 4 weeks before your new exam date.
Week 8 (2–8 Nov): the course ends on Wednesday, then switch to exam mode
  • Basics: do the 36-question check again and repeat every lesson you still miss. Practice gym drill 8 (exam mix), then redo the drill you found hardest.
  • Words: Words 6: free time, media, time words. Then review all ⭐ words.
  • From Thursday: read the whole exam section again (every task, every trap).
  • Goal: 30 of 36 or better in the check.

🎯 Weeks 9–12: exam training (after the course)

Week 9 (9–15 Nov): reading + letters
  • All 4 workouts in the Practice section, the reading strategies and the Sprachbausteine method.
  • 3 letters, 30 minutes each: one formal complaint, one informal, one request.
  • 30 minutes of listening every day, using the listening strategies. Speaking parts 1 + 2 with your partner.
  • Goal: every letter covers all 4 points in 30 minutes.
Week 10 (16–22 Nov): listening + speaking
  • Practice test 3 (a new test, with the exam clock). Then re-study your 2 weakest parts.
  • All 3 speaking parts with your partner, 3 times this week. Learn the rescue phrases by heart.
  • Read the phrases on the cheat sheet every day.
  • Goal: talk through all 3 speaking parts (about 15 minutes) without stopping.
Week 11 (23–29 Nov): a full test run, like the real exam
  • Practice test 4, exactly like the real exam. Then fix the 2 weakest parts.
  • 3 letters, and a speaking simulation every day with a timer.
  • Goal: 60% or more in the practice test.
Week 12 (30 Nov – exam day): rest, repeat, sleep
  • No new material. Only the cheat sheet, your personal mistake list, and the exam-day checklist in the exam section.
  • Light listening every day. Sleep well. A tired brain loses more points than a small grammar gap.
From week 9, the exam is your only job: about 2 hours a day. Four weeks of practice tests, letters and speaking training usually add more points than anything else you can do.

🎧 Listening practice: real audio every day

This guide cannot play audio. But listening (Hörverstehen) is worth 75 points, a third of the written exam. So real audio is part of your plan every day. All sources below are free. You don't need all of them: your listening minutes are one or two items from this list.

WhatWhyWhen in the plan
Official telc Deutsch B1 Übungstest (free PDF + MP3 from telc.net)The most important practice: real exam tasks, real audio, real timing, with an answer key.Practice test 1 in week 4. Later again, only for timing practice
DW „Nicos Weg“ B1 (free video course, learngerman.dw.com)A free B1 course told as a story, with clear speech, subtitles and exercises after each video.3–4 short episodes a week, weeks 1–8
Nachrichtenleicht (nachrichtenleicht.de)The news in simple German, audio + text. A gentle start.A few times a week from week 1
DW „Top-Thema mit Vokabeln“Short B1-level audio texts with a vocabulary list: listening and words in one.2 a week from week 4
DW „Langsam gesprochene Nachrichten“ (slowly spoken news, with transcript)Real news read slowly. DW marks it as level B2–C1, so it's hard at first. Listen once, then read the transcript and listen again.10 minutes a day from week 5. If it's far too hard, stay with Nachrichtenleicht
Easy German (YouTube)Real street interviews with German + English subtitles. Trains you for natural, fast speech.2–3 videos a week
Reading feels like progress, but the exam also tests listening, writing and speaking. A simple rule: for every hour of reading, spend one hour listening, writing or speaking out loud.

Not sure where to start? Do the 36-question check first. It links every wrong answer to its lesson. Your teacher's grammar words (Partizip II, Hilfsverb, Nebensatz …) are translated in the glossary.
Don't do all 36 at once. Do 1–2 lessons a day. Start with the ones that match what your course is doing this week. Anything about verb forms (Partizip II, hatte, wurde, modal verbs) has its own big section: the Verb forms centre.

🩺 Which lessons do I need? — the 36-question check

You learned all these rules in A1 and A2 — and some of them have gone out of your head. That is normal! This check has one question for each lesson (lesson 1 to 36). It takes about 10 minutes.

  1. Do all 36 questions. Don't look anything up — a wrong answer is useful information.
  2. Wrong answer? The feedback shows a link to the lesson. Write down the lesson number. e.g. 6, 13, 16, 25
  3. Do those lessons first. One lesson ≈ 10 minutes. Skip the lessons you got right.
  4. Do the check again in 2 weeks. Your list should be shorter.
▶️ Start the check 36 questions
✍️ The big check — one question per lesson 36 items

Choose the right option, or type the missing word (the word in brackets tells you what to use).

  1. Mein Bruder ___ 25 Jahre alt. (My brother is 25 years old.)
  2. Du ___ sehr gut. (kochen) (You cook very well.)
  3. Morgen ___ zum Arzt. (Tomorrow I'm going to the doctor.)
  4. ___ Kinder spielen im Park. (das Kind, plural) (The children are playing in the park.)
  5. Ich habe heute ___ Zeit. (I have no time today.)
  6. Ich brauche ___ Termin beim Arzt. (der Termin) (I need an appointment at the doctor's.)
  7. Anna besucht heute ___ Bruder. (Anna is visiting her brother today.)
  8. Er ___ jeden Tag mit dem Bus zur Arbeit. (fahren) (He goes to work by bus every day.)
  9. Mein Kollege ___ sehr gut kochen. (können) (My colleague can cook very well.)
  10. Wann ___ der Zug in Köln an? (When does the train arrive in Cologne?)
  11. ___ mir bitte das Salz! (geben, to a friend) (Pass me the salt, please!)
  12. Mein neuer Deutschkurs beginnt ___ Oktober. (My new German course starts in October.)
  13. Ich habe gestern zwei Stunden Deutsch ___ . (lernen, ge-word) (Yesterday I studied German for two hours.)
  14. Ich ___ gestern mit dem Zug nach Hamburg gefahren. (Yesterday I went to Hamburg by train.)
  15. Gestern ___ ich leider keine Zeit. (haben, short past) (Unfortunately I had no time yesterday.)
  16. Ich helfe ___ Frau mit dem Koffer. (die Frau) (I'm helping the woman with the suitcase.)
  17. Abends fahre ich mit ___ U-Bahn nach Hause. (die U-Bahn) (In the evening I take the underground home.)
  18. Ich gehe jetzt ___ Supermarkt. (der Supermarkt) (I'm going to the supermarket now.)
  19. Mein Kollege interessiert ___ für Fußball. (My colleague is interested in football.)
  20. Ich kann heute nicht kommen, weil ___ . (I can't come today because I'm ill.)
  21. Ich weiß nicht, ___ der Supermarkt heute offen ist. (I don't know whether the supermarket is open today.)
  22. Es regnet, ___ bleibe ich heute zu Hause. (It's raining, so I'm staying at home today.)
  23. Berlin ist ___ als Köln. (groß, compare) (Berlin is bigger than Cologne.)
  24. Ich suche eine ___ Wohnung. (I'm looking for a cheap flat.)
  25. Wenn ich mehr Geld hätte, ___ ich eine größere Wohnung mieten. (If I had more money, I would rent a bigger flat.)
  26. Ich warte ___ einen Anruf vom Arzt. (I'm waiting for a call from the doctor.)
  27. Die Jacke kostet ___ Euro. (47 — write it in words) (The jacket costs 47 euros.)
  28. ___ kommst du? – Aus Bangladesch. (Where are you from? – From Bangladesh.)
  29. In meiner Straße ___ es drei Cafés. (There are three cafés in my street.)
  30. Ich telefoniere jeden Sonntag mit ___ Mutter. (I talk to my mother on the phone every Sunday.)
  31. Kannst du ___ Kind bitte den Ball geben? (das Kind) (Can you please give the child the ball?)
  32. Hast du einen Stift für mich? – Nein, ich habe leider ___ . (Do you have a pen for me? – No, sorry, I don't have one.)
  33. Ich habe heute keine Lust, für alle ___ . (kochen, with zu — 2 words) (I don't feel like cooking for everyone today.)
  34. ___ ich ein Kind war, habe ich in Dhaka gewohnt. (When I was a child, I lived in Dhaka.)
  35. Es ist ___ 7 Uhr. Wir haben noch viel Zeit. (It's only 7 o'clock. We still have lots of time.)
  36. Der Kollege, ___ ich jeden Tag im Bus sehe, heißt Tom. (The colleague whom I see on the bus every day is called Tom.)
Finished? Count your mistakes. 0–5 wrong: great — just repeat those lessons. 6–15 wrong: do one or two lessons a day. More than 15: start at lesson 1 and go in order — the lessons build on each other.

📖 Grammar words your teacher uses — German · our nickname · English

Your teacher talks about grammar with German words: „Das ist Präteritum.“ (That is the Präteritum.) „Achtung, Dativ!“ (Careful, Dativ!) This card translates them. Each row gives the German term, the nickname we use in this guide, a plain-English meaning, a tiny example and where to learn it.

If you speak Bengali — two mirrors that make German easier:
1 · Verb at the end. Bengali puts the verb at the END of the sentence: আমি ভাত খাই (ami bhat khai) = "I rice eat". German does that too — but only in the weil / dass / wenn part: …, weil ich Reis esse. (… because I eat rice.) In a normal German sentence the verb stays in seat 2: Ich esse Reis. (I eat rice.)
2 · Two past forms. Bengali has খেলাম (khelam, "I ate") and খেয়েছি (kheyechi, "I have eaten"). German also has two past forms: ich aß (story past) and ich habe gegessen (spoken past with a ge-word). But careful: in German both mean "I ate" in everyday talk. The difference is speaking vs writing, not the meaning — so when you speak, say Ich habe gegessen. (I ate.)
A1 1 · Personal pronouns + sein & haben (present) ich bin · du hast

You will learn: the little "people words" (I, you, she …) and the two most important verbs in German: sein (to be) and haben (to have).

The rule: A pronoun is a short word that stands for a person or a thing (I, you, she, it …). Every pronoun needs the right verb form: ich bin, du bist, er ist. sein and haben don't follow the normal pattern — learn their 6 forms by heart.

Who is who? The pronouns

GermanEnglishUsed for
ichIyourself (small i — only capital at the start of a sentence)
duyouone friend, family, a child, classmates
erhea man (and der-words: der Bus → er)
sieshea woman (and die-words: die Tür → sie)
esitdas-words (das Kind → es)
wirweme + other people
ihryou alltwo or more friends / family members
sietheya group of people or things
Sieyou (polite)doctor, boss, teacher, office — one person or many. Always a capital S!

sie, sie or Sie? Look at the verb and the capital S

You see …It meansExampleEnglish
sie + ist / hat (the er-form of the verb)sheMeine Kollegin? Sie ist krank.My colleague? She is sick.
sie + sind / haben (the wir-form of the verb)theyDie Kinder? Sie sind in der Schule.The children? They are at school.
Sie with a capital S in the middle of a sentence + the wir-form of the verbyou (polite)Haben Sie einen Termin?Do you have an appointment?
The first word of a sentence always has a capital letter, so "Sie sind …" can mean "they are" or "you are". Then only the situation tells you.

sein and haben — all 6 persons

Personsein (to be)haben (to have)
ichbinhabe
dubisthast

Ich bin müde, aber ich habe heute Deutschkurs.I'm tired, but I have German class today.
Du bist neu hier, oder?You're new here, right?
Mein Kollege hat Fieber. Er ist krank.My colleague has a fever. He is sick.
Seid ihr morgen im Kurs?Are you (all) in the course tomorrow?ihr seid (with d) = you all are. Don't mix it up with "seit" (since).
Kommen Sie morgen? — Kommen sie morgen?Are you (polite) coming tomorrow? — Are they coming tomorrow?Same sound, but in writing the capital S shows the polite "you".
Wir haben eine kleine Wohnung.We have a small flat.
Classic mistakes:
✗ Ich bin Hunger. → ✓ Ich habe Hunger. (I am hungry — in German you "have" hunger. Same with Durst, Angst, Zeit, Kopfschmerzen.)
✗ Ich habe 30 Jahre. → ✓ Ich bin 30 (Jahre alt). (I am 30 years old — your age is something you "are".)
Memory trickBig S = big respect. Capital Sie is for people you'd shake hands with formally: the doctor, your boss, the lady at the office. And your body feelings go in a bag you carry: you have Hunger, Durst, Angst. Your age is you: ich bin 30.

A1 2 · Regular verbs: the present-tense endings ich lerne · du lernst

You will learn: how to glue the right ending onto a normal verb for each person (the "now-form", Präsens).

The rule: Take the verb from the dictionary (lernen) and cut off -en. What is left is the stem — the body of the verb (lern). Then add the ending for the person: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.
PersonEndingmachen (do/make)wohnen (live)lernen (learn)
ich-emachewohnelerne
du-stmachstwohnstlernst
er / sie / es-tmachtwohntlernt
wir-enmachenwohnenlernen
ihr-tmachtwohntlernt
sie / Sie-enmachenwohnenlernen

Two small special groups

Stem ends in …What happensForms
-t / -d
arbeiten, finden, warten, reden
(work, find, wait, talk)		add an extra e before -st and -t (so you can say it)du arbeitest, er arbeitet, ihr arbeitet
du findest, er findet, ihr findet
-s / -ß / -z
heißen, tanzen, reisen
(be called, dance, travel)		du only adds -t (the s sound is already there)du heißt, du tanzt, du reist
Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Deutschland.I have been living in Germany for two years.
Lernst du auch für die Prüfung?Are you also studying for the exam?
Meine Frau arbeitet im Krankenhaus.My wife works at the hospital.Stem arbeit- ends in -t → extra e: arbeit-e-t.
Wie heißt du? — Ich heiße Sami.What's your name? — My name is Sami.Stem heiß- ends in ß → du only adds -t: du heißt.
Die Fahrkarte kostet zehn Euro.The ticket costs ten euros.
Wir kochen heute zusammen.We are cooking together today.

✗ du arbeitst → ✓ du arbeitest
✗ du heißst → ✓ du heißt
✗ er lernen → ✓ er lernt (only wir / sie / Sie use the -en form)
Memory trickChant the endings like a drum beat: e – st – t – en – t – en. And spot the twins: er & ihr both end in -t (er lernt, ihr lernt); wir & sie/Sie look exactly like the dictionary word (lernen). So really you only need three endings: ich -e, du -st and the -t twins.

Type or choose the correct verb form.

  2. Er ___ in einem Hotel. (arbeiten) (He works in a hotel.)
  3. Wie ___ du? (What is your name?)
  4. Wir ___ in Berlin. (We live in Berlin.)
  5. Ihr ___ zu schnell. (reden) (You all talk too fast.)

A1 3 · Word order: verb in position 2, questions Heute arbeite ich.

You will learn: where the verb sits in a normal sentence, in a W-question and in a yes/no question.

The rule: In a normal sentence the verb (the form that changes with the person: ich arbeite, du arbeitest) always sits in position 2 — the "VIP seat 2". In a yes/no question the verb jumps to position 1.

A "position" is one idea, not one word: am Montag is two words but one position.

Statements: the verb never leaves seat 2

Position 1Verb (position 2)RestEnglish
Icharbeiteheute bis 17 Uhr.I'm working until 5 pm today.
Heutearbeiteich bis 17 Uhr.Today I'm working until 5 pm.
Am Montaghabeich einen Arzttermin.On Monday I have a doctor's appointment.
Mein Bruderwohntin Hamburg.My brother lives in Hamburg.

If something else (a time word like heute, morgen, am Montag) takes seat 1, the person (ich, du …) jumps behind the verb, into seat 3.

Questions

TypePosition 1Position 2RestEnglish
W-questionWowohnstdu?Where do you live?
W-questionWasmachstdu am Wochenende?What are you doing at the weekend?
yes/no questionKommstdumorgen zum Kurs?Are you coming to the course tomorrow?
W-words: wer (who), was (what), wo (where), wann (when), warum (why), wie (how). W-word first → verb second → person third. No W-word → the verb goes first. More question words (woher = where from, wie viel = how much, welcher = which …) → lesson 28.
Am Wochenende besuche ich meine Tante.At the weekend I visit my aunt."Am Wochenende" takes seat 1 → verb stays in seat 2 → ich moves to seat 3.
Leider habe ich keine Zeit.Unfortunately I have no time.
Nach dem Kurs gehe ich einkaufen.After the course I'm going shopping.
Wann fährt der Zug nach München?When does the train to Munich leave?
Hast du einen Stift?Do you have a pen?Yes/no question → the verb is in seat 1.
Classic mistakes:
✗ Heute ich arbeite. → ✓ Heute arbeite ich. (Today I'm working.)
✗ Wo du wohnst? → ✓ Wo wohnst du? (Where do you live?)
Memory trickThe verb is a VIP with seat number 2. Whoever sits in seat 1 — ich, heute, leider, am Montag — the VIP never gives up seat 2. The person just moves to seat 3. In a yes/no question the VIP is so excited that it jumps to the front: Hast du …?
✍️ Quick check — word order 5 items

Choose the right order or type the verb in the right form.

  1. Heute ___ Deutsch. (Today I'm learning German.)
  2. Wo ___ ? (Where do you live?)
  3. Am Montag ___ ich zum Arzt. (gehen) (On Monday I'm going to the doctor.)
  4. ___ du morgen Zeit? (haben) (Do you have time tomorrow?)
  5. Morgen ___ meine Schwester. (kommen) (My sister is coming tomorrow.)

A1 4 · Nouns: der/die/das, plural, ein/eine der Tisch · die Tür · das Buch

You will learn: why every German noun has der, die or das, how the plural works, and when to say ein or eine.

The rule: A noun is a word for a person, thing, place or idea (Lehrer, Tisch, Stadt, Liebe). In German every noun starts with a capital letter and has an article: der, die or das. In the plural it is always die — but the noun itself changes.

The colours in this guide: der blue = masculine · die red = feminine · das green = neuter (neither) · die grey = plural. The gender is often not logical: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter! So always learn a noun with its article.

the → a/an: der, die, das → ein, eine

Article (the)a / anExampleEnglish
dereinder Tisch → ein Tischthe table → a table
dieeinedie Tür → eine Türthe door → a door
daseindas Buch → ein Buchthe book → a book
die (plural)— (nothing!)die Bücher → Bücherthe books → books

5 common plural patterns

PatternSingular → pluralEnglish
+ e (sometimes + ¨)der Tag → die Tage · der Stuhl → die Stühleday · chair
+ er (+ ¨ if possible)das Kind → die Kinder · das Buch → die Bücherchild · book
+ n / + endie Lampe → die Lampen · die Wohnung → die Wohnungenlamp · flat
+ sdas Auto → die Autos · das Handy → die Handyscar · mobile phone
no ending (sometimes + ¨)der Lehrer → die Lehrer · der Bruder → die Brüderteacher · brother
Good news: most die-words make their plural with -n / -en (die Frau → die Frauen). And the plural article is always the same: die.

Gender hints that really work

If the noun …ArticleExamplesEnglish
ends in -ung, -heit, -keit, -iondiedie Wohnung, die Gesundheit, die Möglichkeit, die Informationflat · health · possibility · information
ends in -chen (small things)dasdas Mädchen, das Brötchengirl · bread roll
is a day, month or seasonderder Montag, der Mai, der WinterMonday · May · winter
is made of two nounsthe last word decidesdie Tür + der Schlüssel = der Türschlüssel
das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür		door key · front door
Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr.The course starts at nine o'clock.
Im Zimmer steht ein Tisch.There is a table in the room.
Ich habe zwei Brüder und eine Schwester.I have two brothers and a sister.der Bruder → die Brüder (no ending, but ü). die Schwester → eine Schwester.
Die Kinder sind in der Schule.The children are at school.Plural → always die.
Der Wohnungsschlüssel ist weg!The flat key is gone!die Wohnung + der Schlüssel → the last word decides → der. (The little s in the middle is just glue between the two words.)
Classic mistakes:
✗ Das sind ein Bücher. → ✓ Das sind Bücher. (These are books. — ein has no plural, just like English "a books" is impossible.)
✗ Ich habe ein auto. → ✓ Ich habe ein Auto. (I have a car. — Nouns always start with a capital letter.)
Memory trickPaint every new noun in its colour in your head: a blue table (der Tisch), a red door (die Tür), a green book (das Buch). Never learn "Tisch" alone — learn it like a full name: der Tisch, die Tische.

  2. ___ Brötchen ist frisch. (The bread roll is fresh.)

A1 5 · Saying "no": nicht or kein? kein Auto · nicht heute

You will learn: when to say kein and when to say nicht, where nicht goes, and the magic answer Doch!

The rule: Use kein before a noun that has ein/eine or no article. Use nicht for everything else (verbs, adjectives, der/die/das-nouns, names, places, times).
  1. Is there a noun with ein / eine? Yes → kein. ein Auto → kein Auto
  2. Is there a noun (not a name) with no article at all? Yes → kein. Zeit → keine Zeit
  3. Anything else? → nicht. Ich komme heute nicht. (I'm not coming today.)

From "yes" to "no"

PositiveNegativeEnglish (negative)
Ich habe ein Auto.Ich habe kein Auto.I don't have a car.
Ich habe eine Frage.Ich habe keine Frage.I don't have a question.
Ich trinke Kaffee.Ich trinke keinen Kaffee.I don't drink coffee.
Wir haben Kinder.Wir haben keine Kinder.We don't have children.
Ich kenne den Mann.Ich kenne den Mann nicht.I don't know the man.
Die Wohnung ist groß.Die Wohnung ist nicht groß.The flat isn't big.

kein gets the same endings as ein — plus a plural form: kein Tisch, keine Tür, kein Buch, keine Bücher. For a der-word that is "hit" by the action (the Akkusativ, see lesson 6): keinen Kaffee.

Where does nicht go?

nicht goes …ExampleEnglish
at the end (the whole action is "no")Er arbeitet heute nicht.He isn't working today.
before an adjective (describing word)Das Essen ist nicht gut.The food isn't good.
before a placeIch wohne nicht in München.I don't live in Munich.
before the second verb at the endIch kann heute nicht kommen.I can't come today.

Doch! — "yes" to a "no" question

QuestionAnswerEnglish
Kommst du mit?Ja. / Nein.Are you coming along? — Yes. / No.
Kommst du nicht mit?Doch! / Nein.Aren't you coming along? — Yes, I am! / No, I'm not.
Tut mir leid, ich habe heute keine Zeit.Sorry, I don't have time today.
Ich trinke keinen Alkohol.I don't drink alcohol.der Alkohol, no article → kein; it is the thing you drink (Akkusativ, lesson 6) → keinen.
Der Bus kommt nicht.The bus isn't coming."der Bus" has der, not ein → nicht.
Die Wohnung ist nicht teuer.The flat isn't expensive.
Hast du keinen Hunger? — Doch, ich habe Hunger!Aren't you hungry? — Yes, I am hungry!
Classic mistakes:
✗ Ich habe nicht Zeit. → ✓ Ich habe keine Zeit.
✗ Ich habe nicht ein Auto. → ✓ Ich habe kein Auto.
✗ "Hast du keine Zeit?" — "Ja!" (confusing!) → ✓ "Doch!" (= yes, I do have time)
Memory trickkein = k + ein. If you could put ein (or nothing) in front of the noun, just add a k: ein Auto → kein Auto. Everything else gets nicht. And Doch! is a "no-killer": it kills the "not" in the question.

  2. Das Wetter ist ___ gut. (The weather isn't good.)

  4. Ich habe ___ Kinder. (no …) (I don't have children.)

A1 6 · Akkusativ: den / einen / mich / ihn Ich brauche einen Stift.

You will learn: what the Akkusativ is, the one small change it makes, and the pronouns mich, dich, ihn …

The rule: The Akkusativ A is the person or thing the action "hits" (I buy a table, I see him). The doer (the subject — who or what the sentence is about) is in the Nominativ N. For nouns, only der-words change their article: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen. die, das and plural stay the same.

To find it, ask Wen? (whom?) for people or Was? (what?) for things: Ich sehe den Bus. → Was sehe ich? → den Bus. (I see the bus. → What do I see? → the bus.)

N the doerA "hit" by the action
derder / ein / kein Kaffeeden / einen / keinen Kaffee
diedie / eine / keine Taschedie / eine / keine Tasche
dasdas / ein / kein Brotdas / ein / kein Brot
diedie / — / keine Äpfeldie / — / keine Äpfel

Verbs that love the Akkusativ

VerbExampleEnglish
habenIch habe einen Termin.I have an appointment.
brauchenIch brauche einen Stift.I need a pen.
möchtenIch möchte einen Tee, bitte.I'd like a tea, please.
kaufenWir kaufen den Tisch.We're buying the table.
sehenSiehst du den Bus?Do you see the bus?
suchenSie sucht den Schlüssel.She's looking for the key.
es gibtEs gibt einen Supermarkt in der Nähe.There is a supermarket nearby.

Pronouns in the Akkusativ

NAEnglish
ichmichme
dudichyou
erihnhim (or "it" for a der-word)
siesieher
esesit
wirunsus
ihreuchyou all
siesiethem
SieSieyou (polite)
Der Kuchen ist lecker. Ich nehme den Kuchen.The cake is tasty. I'll take the cake.First sentence: the cake is the subject (the sentence is about it) → Nominativ → der. Second: I take it → it is "hit" → den.
Ich brauche einen Termin beim Arzt.I need an appointment at the doctor's.
Wir suchen eine Wohnung.We're looking for a flat.die Wohnung → no change: eine.
Kennst du ihn? — Ja, er ist mein Nachbar.Do you know him? — Yes, he's my neighbour.
Ich rufe dich morgen an.I'll call you tomorrow.
Hier gibt es keinen Parkplatz.There's no parking space here.
Classic mistakes:
✗ Ich habe ein Termin. → ✓ Ich habe einen Termin. (I have an appointment.)
✗ Ich möchte ein Kaffee. → ✓ Ich möchte einen Kaffee. (I'd like a coffee.)
✗ Ich liebe du. → ✓ Ich liebe dich. (I love you.)
Memory trickOnly the man reacts when he is hit: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen, er → ihn. The others (die, das, plural) don't even notice. Masculine Akkusativ always has an n.

A1 7 · Possessive words: mein, dein, sein, ihr … mein Bruder · meine Schwester

You will learn: how to say my, your, his, her, our, their — and which ending to put on them.

The rule: Who owns it picks the word (mein, sein, ihr …). The thing that is owned picks the ending — exactly the same endings as ein / kein: -e for die-words and plural, -en for a der-word in the Akkusativ.
OwnerWordEnglish
ichmeinmy
dudeinyour (friend, family)
erseinhis
sieihrher
esseinits
wirunserour
ihreueryour (you all)
sieihrtheir
SieIhryour (polite) — capital I!

The endings (same as ein / kein)

N the doerA "hit" by the action
dermein Brudermeinen Bruder
diemeine Schwestermeine Schwester
dasmein Kindmein Kind
diemeine Elternmeine Eltern
euer drops its middle e when an ending comes: euer Lehrer, but eure Kinder, euren Lehrer.

Dativ forms (the form after mit, bei, zu …): mit meinem Bruder (with my brother), mit meiner Mutter (with my mother) → lesson 30.

Meine Eltern wohnen in Dhaka.My parents live in Dhaka.Plural → meine.
Ich besuche morgen meinen Bruder.I'm visiting my brother tomorrow.der Bruder is "hit" by besuchen → Akkusativ → meinen.
Frau Klein und ihr Mann sind sehr nett.Ms Klein and her husband are very nice.The owner is a woman → ihr.
Tom sucht seine Brille.Tom is looking for his glasses.Owner = Tom → sein. die Brille → ending -e → seine.
Wo ist euer Lehrer? — Unser Lehrer ist krank.Where is your teacher? — Our teacher is sick.
Wie ist Ihr Name, bitte?What is your name, please?Capital I → polite "your" (at the doctor's, at the office).
Classic mistakes:
✗ Anna und sein Mann → ✓ Anna und ihr Mann (the owner Anna is a woman → ihr)
✗ Ich besuche mein Bruder. → ✓ Ich besuche meinen Bruder.
Memory trickAsk two questions. 1. Who owns it? → that picks the word (Anna → ihr, Tom → sein). 2. What is owned? → that picks the ending (die Brille → seine Brille). And ihr is a Swiss army knife: ihr = you all, ihr = her, ihr = their, Ihr = your (polite).

  2. Tom ruft ___ Mutter an. (Tom calls his mother.)

A1 8 · Verbs that change their vowel (fahren → fährt) du fährst · er isst

You will learn: which common verbs change a vowel (a, e, au) in the now-form — and for which persons.

The rule: Some verbs change their vowel only with du and er / sie / es. The endings stay normal (-st, -t). ich, wir, ihr, sie/Sie keep the normal vowel.
ChangeVerb → er / sie / esEnglish
e → iessen → isst · geben → gibt · helfen → hilft · nehmen → nimmt · sprechen → spricht · treffen → trifft · vergessen → vergissteat · give · help · take · speak · meet · forget
e → ielesen → liest · sehen → sieht · empfehlen → empfiehltread · see · recommend
a → äfahren → fährt · schlafen → schläft · tragen → trägt · waschen → wäscht · einladen → lädt … eindrive/go · sleep · carry/wear · wash · invite
au → äulaufen → läuftrun / walk

Two little extras: du isst (not "issst" — the stem already ends in s, so du only adds -t). nehmen also changes its consonants: du nimmst, er nimmt. And einladen gets no extra e (even though the stem ends in d): du lädst ein, er lädt ein.

A1 9 · Modal verbs in the present (können, müssen …) ich kann · du musst

You will learn: the modal verbs you need every day, their forms, and where the second verb goes. There are 6 modal verbs — können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, mögen — + möchten (the polite "would like", which comes from mögen).

The rule: A modal verb is a helper that adds a "mood" to an action: can, must, want … In a statement it sits in position 2 (in a yes/no question: position 1). The action verb goes to the very end in its dictionary form (the infinitive: lernen, kommen). And: ich and er/sie/es are the same form with no ending (ich kann, er kann).
ModalEnglishFeeling
könnencan, be able toI'm able / it's possible
müssenmust, have tono choice
wollenwant tomy strong wish / plan
dürfenmay, be allowed topermission
sollenshould, be supposed tosomeone else wants it (doctor, boss)
mögenlikeI like it — mostly with a noun: Ich mag Kaffee. (I like coffee.)
möchtenwould like (to)polite wish: Ich möchte einen Kaffee. (I would like a coffee.)

All forms

Personkönnenmüssenwollen
ichkannmusswill
dukannstmusstwillst
er / sie / eskannmusswill
wirkönnenmüssenwollen
ihrkönntmüsstwollt
sie / Siekönnenmüssenwollen
Persondürfensollenmöchten
ichdarfsollmöchte

er / sie / esdarfsollmöchte
wirdürfensollenmöchten
ihrdürftsolltmöchtet
sie / Siedürfensollenmöchten
Notice: ich, du, er (the "one person" forms) often get a different vowel: können → kann, müssen → muss, dürfen → darf, wollen → will, mögen → mag. wir, ihr, sie/Sie keep the vowel of the dictionary form. (möchte is a little different: it ends in -e, but ich and er are still the same.)
mögen (to like): ich mag, du magst, er / sie / es mag, wir mögen, ihr mögt, sie / Sie mögen. It is mostly used with a noun, without a second verb: Ich mag Kaffee. (I like coffee.) · Magst du Fußball? (Do you like football?) For a polite wish, use möchten: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. (I would like a coffee, please.)

The sentence bracket: modal in seat 2, infinitive at the end

Position 1Modal (pos. 2)MiddleEND = infinitiveEnglish
Ichmussheute bis 18 Uhrarbeiten.I have to work until 6 pm today.
Morgenkannich leider nichtkommen.Unfortunately I can't come tomorrow.
Hierdarfman nichtparken.You're not allowed to park here. (man = "you" / people in general)
Ich kann gut kochen.I can cook well.
Musst du am Samstag arbeiten?Do you have to work on Saturday?
Der Arzt sagt, ich soll mehr Wasser trinken.The doctor says I should drink more water.sollen = somebody else (the doctor) wants it.
Ich möchte einen Termin machen.I would like to make an appointment.
Wir wollen im Sommer nach Italien fahren.We want to go to Italy in the summer.
Könnt ihr mir helfen?Can you (all) help me?
Classic mistakes and traps:
✗ ich kanne / er kannt → ✓ ich kann / er kann (no ending!)
✗ Ich muss arbeite. → ✓ Ich muss arbeiten. (the second verb is always the dictionary form)
Trap 1: Du musst nicht kommen. = You don't have to come (it's OK to stay home). Du darfst nicht kommen. = You must not come (it's forbidden!).
Trap 2: Ich will … = I want …, NOT "I will". Ich will ein Eis. = I want an ice cream.

werden = will (the future): Ich werde morgen arbeiten. (I will work tomorrow.) But werden is NOT a modal verb — see Verb forms centre · werden.

Memory trickich and er are naked twins — no ending, no clothes: ich kann – er kann, ich muss – er muss, ich will – er will. And the modal is a pair of hands: one hand in seat 2 (kann), the other hand at the very end (kommen), holding the sentence between them.

A1 10 · Separable and inseparable verbs ich rufe dich an · ich verstehe

You will learn: why verbs like anrufen break into two pieces — and which verbs never break.

Some verbs have a small front piece (grammar word: prefix): anrufen, aufstehen, einkaufen. The rest of the verb is the normal verb (rufen, stehen, kaufen).

The rule: In a normal sentence the verb sits in VIP seat 2 and the front piece jumps to the very end: Ich rufe dich an. But the front pieces be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver-, zer- are glued on — they never jump.

The 7 separable verbs you need every day

VerbMeaningNormal sentence (now-form)

einkaufento go shoppingWir kaufen am Samstag ein.
We go shopping on Saturday.
fernsehento watch TVEr sieht jeden Abend fern.
He watches TV every evening.
mitkommento come alongKommst du mit?
Are you coming along?
abholento pick upIch hole dich vom Bahnhof ab.
I'll pick you up from the station.
anfangento startDer Kurs fängt um neun Uhr an.
The course starts at nine.

One verb, three situations

SituationWhat happensExample
NOW-FORMfront piece jumps to the endIch rufe dich morgen an.

WITH A MODALmodal (muss, kann …) in seat 2, verb stays whole at the endIch muss dich morgen anrufen.

PERFEKT(the spoken past, see lesson 13) ge goes in the middleIch habe dich angerufen.

The glued front pieces (never split)

ent-entschuldigen (to excuse)Entschuldigen Sie!Er hat sich entschuldigt.
ge- / zer-gefallen (to please) · zerstören (to destroy)Das gefällt mir.Das hat mir gefallen.

English: I visit my aunt · I don't understand that · She explains the rule · He recommends the restaurant · Excuse me! · I like that. — Perfekt: I visited her · I didn't understand that · She explained the rule · He recommended it · He apologised · I liked that.

Ich stehe jeden Tag um sechs Uhr auf.I get up at six o'clock every day.
Kommst du heute Abend mit?Are you coming along this evening?
Ich kann dich morgen vom Bahnhof abholen.I can pick you up from the station tomorrow.With a modal (kann), the modal takes seat 2 and the verb waits at the end in ONE piece: abholen.
Wir haben gestern im Supermarkt eingekauft.We went shopping at the supermarket yesterday.Perfekt: ge goes between the front piece and the verb: ein-ge-kauft.
Ich verstehe die Frage nicht.I don't understand the question.ver- is glued on. It never jumps to the end.
Die Lehrerin erklärt uns die Hausaufgabe.The teacher explains the homework to us.
Classic mistake:
✗ Ich anrufe dich morgen. → ✓ Ich rufe dich morgen an.
✗ Ich habe dich geanrufen. → ✓ Ich habe dich angerufen. (ge sits in the middle)
✗ Ich stehe das nicht ver. → ✓ Ich verstehe das nicht. (ver- never jumps)
Memory trickSay the verb out loud and listen. Loud front = loose front: AN-rufen, AUF-stehen, EIN-kaufen — the stress is on the front piece, so it can jump away. Quiet front = glued front: ver-STE-hen, be-SU-chen, er-KLÄ-ren — the stress is on the verb, so the front piece stays.

Type the missing word or tap the right answer.

  1. Ich ___ jeden Tag um 7 Uhr auf. (aufstehen) (I get up at 7 every day.)
  2. Der Kurs ___ um 9 Uhr an. (The course starts at 9.)

A1 11 · Giving instructions: the imperative Komm! · Kommen Sie!

You will learn: how to tell someone to do something — a friend, a group, or a stranger (polite).

The imperative is simply the order form of a verb: Come! Wait! Take this! In German the verb goes to the front (position 1).

The rule: du → take the du-form, remove du and the ending -st: du kommst → Komm! · ihr → the ihr-form without ihr: Kommt! · Sie → infinitive (the dictionary form, e.g. kommen) + Sie: Kommen Sie!
Verbto one friend (du)to friends (ihr)polite (Sie)
kommenKomm!Kommt!Kommen Sie!
machenMach!Macht!Machen Sie!
wartenWarte!Wartet!Warten Sie!
nehmenNimm!Nehmt!Nehmen Sie!
gebenGib!Gebt!Geben Sie!
sprechenSprich!Sprecht!Sprechen Sie!
lesenLies!Lest!Lesen Sie!
fahrenFahr!Fahrt!Fahren Sie!
schlafenSchlaf!Schlaft!Schlafen Sie!
seinSei!Seid!Seien Sie!
anrufenRuf … an!Ruft … an!Rufen Sie … an!

English: come · do/make · wait · take · give · speak · read · drive · sleep · be · call.

  • warten: the stem (the verb without -en: wart-) ends in -t, so the du-form keeps an -e: Warte! (Wait!)
  • e → i verbs keep the i: du nimmst → Nimm! · du gibst → Gib! · du sprichst → Sprich! · du liest → Lies! (careful: the s stays)
  • a → ä verbs lose the dots: du fährst → Fahr! · du schläfst → Schlaf!
  • sein is special: Sei ruhig! (Be quiet!) · Seid pünktlich! (Be on time!) · Seien Sie bitte vorsichtig! (Please be careful!)
Make it friendly: an order can sound rude. Add a softener: bitte (please), mal (just, quickly), doch (why don't you …).
Mach bitte das Fenster zu! — Please close the window! · Komm doch mit! — Why don't you come along!
Ruf mich heute Abend an!Call me tonight!Separable verb: the front piece an still jumps to the end.
Nehmen Sie die Tabletten dreimal am Tag.Take the tablets three times a day. (the doctor to you)
Sprich bitte langsam!Please speak slowly! (to a friend)sprechen is an e → i verb: du sprichst → Sprich!
Fahr vorsichtig!Drive carefully!du fährst — but the order form has no dots: Fahr!
Kinder, seid bitte leise!Children, please be quiet!
Warten Sie bitte einen Moment.Please wait a moment.
Hilf mir bitte mal!Please give me a hand for a moment!helfen is an e → i verb too: du hilfst → Hilf!
Classic mistake:
✗ Du komm! / ✗ Kommst! → ✓ Komm! (no du, no -st)
✗ Nehm das! → ✓ Nimm das! (e → i stays)
✗ Fähr langsam! → ✓ Fahr langsam! (a → ä does NOT stay)
Memory trickThe du-order is like a text message 📱 — short and fast. Delete "du", delete "-st", press send: du kommst → Komm! · du nimmst → Nimm! And remember: the i stays, the dots go.

  2. ___ bitte langsam, Herr Müller! (Please speak slowly, Mr Müller!)
  3. ___ den Text! (lesen, to a friend) (Read the text!)
  4. ___ vorsichtig, Tom! (Drive carefully, Tom!)

A1 12 · Time words: am, um, im, seit, vor, nach am Montag · um 8 Uhr · im Juli

You will learn: the little words that answer Wann? (When?) — so you can make appointments and talk about your week.

The rule: um = clock time · am = days, dates, parts of the day · im = months and seasons. seit = something started in the past and is still true now → use the now-form.
WordUse it forExamples
umclock timeum 8 Uhr, um halb neun
at 8 o'clock, at half past eight
amdays, dates, parts of the day, weekendam Montag, am 3. Mai, am Abend, am Wochenende
on Monday, on 3rd May, in the evening, at the weekend
immonths, seasonsim Juli, im Winter
in July, in winter
in derthe night (the one part of the day without am!)in der Nacht
at night
von … bisfrom … tovon 9 bis 17 Uhr
from 9 am to 5 pm
abfrom … on (a start)ab Montag
from Monday on
vor Dbefore / agovor dem Essen, vor zwei Jahren
before the meal, two years ago
nach Dafternach der Arbeit, nach dem Kurs
after work, after the course
seit Dsince / for (still going on)seit Montag, seit einem Jahr
since Monday, for a year

am 3. Mai: the dot after the number means "3rd" — say am dritten Mai. D = Dativ: after vor, nach and seit the article changes (der → dem, das → dem, die → der; plural nouns get -n: zwei Jahren). More about the Dativ in lesson 16.

Clock trap: "halb" looks forward!

ClockGermanLiterally
8:00acht Uhreight o'clock
8:15Viertel nach achtquarter past eight
8:30halb neun"half (on the way to) nine" = half past EIGHT
8:45Viertel vor neunquarter to nine
Der Deutschkurs fängt um neun Uhr an.The German course starts at nine o'clock.
Am Wochenende besuche ich meine Familie.At the weekend I visit my family.
Im August habe ich Urlaub.I have my holiday in August.
Nehmen Sie die Tabletten vor dem Essen.Take the tablets before the meal.
Nach der Arbeit gehe ich einkaufen.After work I go shopping.
Ich bin vor zwei Jahren nach Deutschland gekommen.I came to Germany two years ago.English puts "ago" AFTER the time; German puts vor BEFORE it: vor zwei Jahren.
Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch.I have been learning German for a year.I am still learning now → now-form (lerne), not the past. seit + Dativ: ein Jahr → einem Jahr.
Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin.I'm going to Berlin tomorrow.German order: first WHEN (morgen), then WHERE (nach Berlin). English does it the other way round.
Classic mistake:
✗ Ich habe seit zwei Jahren hier gewohnt. (when you still live here) → ✓ Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier.
✗ halb drei = 3:30 → ✓ halb drei = 2:30
✗ Ich fahre nach Berlin morgen. → ✓ Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin. (time before place)
Memory trickThink from small to big: um = the clock hand going round the clock 🕗 (um 8 Uhr) → am = one day (am Montag) → im = a long time you are inside, like a month or a season (im Juli, im Winter). Only the night breaks the rule: in der Nacht.

A1 13 · Perfekt 1: hat + ge-word (regular verbs) ich habe gemacht

You will learn: how to say what you did yesterday — the way Germans really talk about the past.

The Perfekt is the spoken past. Germans use it when they talk and when they write e-mails or messages: "I worked", "I bought", "I have played".

The rule: Build a sandwich 🥪: a form of haben (habe, hast, hat …) in seat 2 + the ge-word at the very end. Everything else goes in the middle.

What is a "ge-word" (Partizip II)?

Look at English: eat → ate → eaten. The word eaten can never stand alone. "I eaten" ✗ is wrong — you need a helper: "I have eaten" ✓. The German ge-word (grammar name: Partizip II) is exactly this kind of word: gemacht (made), gekauft (bought), gespielt (played). It always needs a helper: "Ich gekauft" ✗ → "Ich habe gekauft" ✓.

Good news: "Ich habe gekauft" means BOTH "I bought" and "I have bought". German does not care about that difference. One form for both!

Build the ge-word of a regular verb

Take the infinitive (the dictionary form: machen, kaufen), cut off -en → that is the stem (the core of the verb). Then: ge + stem + t.

InfinitiveStemge-wordEnglish
machenmachgemachtmade / done
kaufenkaufgekauftbought
spielenspielgespieltplayed
lernenlerngelerntlearned
kochenkochgekochtcooked
arbeitenarbeitgearbeitetworked
wartenwartgewartetwaited
redenredgeredettalked

Stem ends in -t or -d? Add -et instead of -t, so you can pronounce it: ge-arbeit-et.

The helper haben — all six persons

PersonHelper (seat 2)ge-word (end)English
ichhabegemachtI did / have done
duhastgemachtyou did
er / sie / eshatgemachthe / she / it did
wirhabengemachtwe did
ihrhabtgemachtyou (all) did
sie / Siehabengemachtthey did / you (polite) did

Only the helper changes. The ge-word never changes: gemacht, gemacht, gemacht.

Ich habe gestern acht Stunden gearbeitet.I worked eight hours yesterday.arbeit- ends in -t, so the ending is -et: ge-arbeit-et.
Wir haben am Samstag Fußball gespielt.We played football on Saturday.
Sie hat im Supermarkt Brot gekauft.She bought bread at the supermarket.
Ich habe eine halbe Stunde auf den Bus gewartet.I waited half an hour for the bus.
Hast du die Hausaufgaben gemacht?Have you done the homework?Yes/no question: the helper jumps to seat 1. The ge-word still stays at the very end.
Was habt ihr im Kurs gelernt?What did you learn in the course?W-question: question word in seat 1, helper in seat 2, ge-word at the end.
Classic mistake:
✗ Ich gekauft Brot. → ✓ Ich habe Brot gekauft. (the ge-word needs a helper)
✗ Ich habe gekauft Brot. → ✓ Ich habe Brot gekauft. (the ge-word goes to the very END)
✗ Er hat gearbeit. → ✓ Er hat gearbeitet. (stem ends in -t → -et)
Memory trick🥪 The helper is the top slice of bread (seat 2), the ge-word is the bottom slice (the very end). Everything else is the filling. No bottom slice = the sandwich falls apart. And the regular ge-word gives the stem a hug: ge-mach-t — ge on the left arm, t on the right arm.

  2. Er hat gestern lange ___. (arbeiten) (He worked late yesterday.)
  3. Wir ___ am Samstag Fußball gespielt. (We played football on Saturday.)

A1 14 · Perfekt 2: ist-verbs and irregular ge-words ich bin gefahren · gegangen

You will learn: which verbs use ist instead of hat, and the ge-words that end in -en.

The rule: Most verbs are in the hat-club. A verb joins the ist-club when the person moves from A to B or changes their state (asleep → awake). Plus four special members: sein, bleiben, passieren, werden.

The ist-club

GroupVerb → PerfektEnglish
🚶 A → Bgehen → ist gegangen · fahren → ist gefahren · fliegen → ist geflogengo · drive/travel · fly
🚶 A → Bkommen → ist gekommen · laufen → ist gelaufen · reisen → ist gereistcome · run/walk · travel
🔄 changeaufstehen → ist aufgestanden · aufwachen → ist aufgewachtget up · wake up
🔄 changeeinschlafen → ist eingeschlafen · sterben → ist gestorbenfall asleep · die
⭐ special 4sein → ist gewesen · bleiben → ist gebliebenbe · stay
⭐ special 4passieren → ist passiert · werden → ist gewordenhappen · become

The helper sein — all six persons

PersonHelper (seat 2)ge-word (end)English
ichbingefahrenI went / have gone
dubistgefahrenyou went
er / sie / esistgefahrenhe / she / it went
wirsindgefahrenwe went
ihrseidgefahrenyou (all) went
sie / Siesindgefahrenthey went / you (polite) went

Irregular ge-words: ending -en, often a new vowel

Irregular verbs do not follow the ge…t pattern. Their ge-word ends in -en, and the vowel in the middle often changes. You have to learn them like words.

VerbPerfektEnglish
gehenist gegangenwent
kommenist gekommencame
trinkenhat getrunkendrank
schreibenhat geschriebenwrote
sehenhat gesehensaw
nehmenhat genommentook
  • Separable verbs: ge goes in the middle: aufgestanden, angekommen.
  • No ge- at all: verbs ending in -ieren (studieren → hat studiert, telefonieren → hat telefoniert) and verbs with be-, ver-, er- (bekommen → hat bekommen, verstehen → hat verstanden, erklären → hat erklärt).
    studieren = to study (at university) · telefonieren = to phone · bekommen = to get, receive (NOT "become"!) · verstehen = to understand · erklären = to explain
Ich bin mit dem Zug nach Hamburg gefahren.I went to Hamburg by train.
Heute bin ich um sechs Uhr aufgestanden.Today I got up at six o'clock.aufstehen = a change (lying → standing) → ist-club. ge sits in the middle: auf-ge-standen.
Am Sonntag sind wir zu Hause geblieben.On Sunday we stayed at home.bleiben = no movement at all, but it is one of the special four → ist.
Was ist passiert?What happened?-ieren verb: no ge-. And passieren is one of the special four → ist.
Er hat seiner Mutter eine E-Mail geschrieben.He wrote an e-mail to his mother.Writing is no travel → hat-club. But schreiben is irregular: ge-schrieb-en.
Ich habe die Frage nicht verstanden.I didn't understand the question.ver- verb → no ge- at the front.
Der Zug ist pünktlich angekommen.The train arrived on time.
Classic mistake:
✗ Ich habe nach Berlin gefahren. → ✓ Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. (A → B = ist-club)
✗ Er hat gegeht. → ✓ Er ist gegangen. (irregular: -en and a new vowel)
✗ Sie hat Medizin gestudiert. → ✓ Sie hat Medizin studiert. (-ieren: no ge-)
Memory trickAsk one question: "Did my body travel, or did I change?" 🚶 Yes → ist. No → hat. Then remember the four VIPs who always get into the ist-club without travelling: sein, bleiben, passieren, werden — "I was, I stayed, it happened, I became."

  2. Ich ___ gestern zu Hause geblieben. (I stayed at home yesterday.)

A1 15 · The short past: war, hatte, musste, konnte ich war · ich hatte · es gab

You will learn: the one-word past forms Germans use every day for "was", "had", "there was", "had to" and "could".

Besides the sandwich, German has a second past: the story past (grammar name: Präteritum). It is ONE word, like English "was" or "ate". In speaking, Germans use it mainly for a few verbs — and those few are exactly the ones you need most.

The rule: For sein, haben, es gibt and the modal verbs (müssen, können …), say the one-word past: war, hatte, es gab, musste, konnte. The ich-form and the er-form are twins: ich war — er war, ich hatte — er hatte (no -t for er!).

war and hatte — all six persons

Personsein → warhaben → hatte
ichwarhatte
duwarsthattest
er / sie / eswarhatte
wirwarenhatten
ihrwarthattet
sie / Siewarenhatten

war = was / were · hatte = had

musste and konnte — all six persons

Personmüssen → musstekönnen → konnte
ichmusstekonnte
dumusstestkonntest
er / sie / esmusstekonnte
wirmusstenkonnten
ihrmusstetkonntet
sie / Siemusstenkonnten

musste = had to · konnte = could / was able to

The other modals work the same way: wollen → wollte (wanted) · dürfen → durfte (was allowed to) · sollen → sollte (was supposed to). And es gibt → es gab (there is → there was).

One-word past vs. ge-word — what is the difference?

Finished past word (stands alone)ge-word (spare part, needs a helper)
ENGLISHI ate.I have eaten.
seinIch war krank.
I was ill.		Ich bin krank gewesen.
I was / have been ill.
habenIch hatte keine Zeit.
I had no time.		Ich habe keine Zeit gehabt.
I had / have had no time.
Both columns are correct German. But "Ich war krank" and "Ich hatte keine Zeit" sound normal and light. The sandwich versions sound heavier. So for sein, haben and the modals: take the short word.
Gestern war ich beim Arzt.Yesterday I was at the doctor's.
Ich hatte starke Kopfschmerzen.I had a bad headache.
Heute gab es im Kurs einen Test.There was a test in the course today.es gibt → es gab. After gab comes the Akkusativ: einen Test.
Ich musste am Samstag arbeiten.I had to work on Saturday.Modal in seat 2, the main verb (arbeiten) waits at the end in its dictionary form.
Warum konntest du gestern nicht kommen?Why couldn't you come yesterday?
Wir wollten ins Kino gehen, aber wir hatten keine Zeit.We wanted to go to the cinema, but we had no time.
Wo warst du am Wochenende?Where were you at the weekend?
Classic mistake:
✗ Gestern habe ich keine Zeit. → ✓ Gestern hatte ich keine Zeit. (habe = now; with gestern you need the past: hatte)
✗ Er hattet keine Zeit. → ✓ Er hatte keine Zeit. (er = ich: no -t)
✗ Ich müsste gestern arbeiten. → ✓ Ich musste gestern arbeiten. (müsste with dots means "would have to")
Memory trickIn the past, the modal verbs lose their dots 🍂: müssen → musste, können → konnte, dürfen → durfte. Past = the dots fell off. And ich and er are twins in the short past: ich war / er war, ich musste / er musste.

  2. Letzte Woche ___ wir keine Zeit. (haben, short past) (Last week we had no time.)

A2 16 · Dativ: dem / der / mir / dir dem Kind · mir · Ihnen

You will learn: the Dativ — the "receiver" form — and the verbs that always want it.

German articles and pronouns change their "costume" to show their job in the sentence. These costumes are called cases. N Nominativ = the doer. A Akkusativ = the thing that gets the action. D Dativ = the receiver: the person something is given to or done for. Its question is Wem? (To whom?)

The rule: In the Dativ, der → dem, das → dem, die → der, and plural die → den (the noun also gets an extra -n, unless it already ends in -n or -s: den Frauen, den Autos). Use the Dativ for the receiver, after Dativ verbs like helfen, and after Dativ prepositions like mit.

Articles

Caseder masculinedie femininedas neuterdie plural
Nder / ein Manndie / eine Fraudas / ein Kinddie Kinder
Aden / einen Manndie / eine Fraudas / ein Kinddie Kinder
Ddem / einem Mannder / einer Fraudem / einem Kindden Kindern

Mann = man · Frau = woman · Kind / Kinder = child / children

Pronouns

N (doer)AD (receiver)English (D)
ichmichmir(to) me
dudichdir(to) you
er / sie / esihn / sie / esihm / ihr / ihm(to) him / her / it
wirunsuns(to) us
ihreucheuch(to) you (all)
sie / Siesie / Sieihnen / Ihnen(to) them / you (polite)

Verbs that always want the Dativ

VerbExampleEnglish
helfenIch helfe dir.I'll help you.
dankenIch danke Ihnen.Thank you. (polite)
gefallenDie Wohnung gefällt mir.I like the flat. (lit. the flat pleases me)
gehörenDas Handy gehört meinem Bruder.The phone belongs to my brother.
schmeckenSchmeckt dir die Suppe?Do you like the soup? (taste)
passenDer Termin passt mir gut.The appointment suits me well.
gratulierenWir gratulieren dir zum Geburtstag.Happy birthday! (we congratulate you)
antwortenBitte antworten Sie mir bis Freitag.Please answer me by Friday.
wehtunMir tut der Kopf weh.My head hurts.

Give-verbs (geben, schenken, zeigen, schicken, erklären = give, give as a present, show, send, explain) have two objects: person = Dativ, thing = Akkusativ. And the famous greeting uses Dativ too: Wie geht es dir / Ihnen? — Mir geht es gut. (How are you? — I'm fine.)

Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel.I give the child an apple.The child receives → Dativ (dem Kind). The apple is given away → Akkusativ (einen Apfel).
Kannst du mir bitte helfen?Can you help me, please?helfen always wants the Dativ: mir, not mich.
Die Ärztin erklärt der Patientin das Problem.The doctor explains the problem to the patient.
Ich kaufe den Kindern ein Eis.I buy the children an ice cream.Dativ plural: den + extra -n on the noun: Kinder → Kindern.
Die neue Wohnung gefällt uns sehr.We like the new flat a lot.
Wie geht es Ihnen, Frau Schmidt?How are you, Mrs Schmidt?
Mir tut der Rücken weh.My back hurts.
Classic mistake:
✗ Ich helfe dich. → ✓ Ich helfe dir.
✗ Ich gefalle die Wohnung. → ✓ Die Wohnung gefällt mir. (the flat is the doer; you are the receiver)
✗ Ich gebe der Kind einen Apfel. → ✓ Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel. (das → dem)
Memory trickPicture the Dativ person with open hands 🤲 — they receive. And listen for the letters: masculine and neuter Dativ end in -m (dem, einem, ihm), feminine Dativ ends in -r (der, einer, ihr). mir, dir, ihr rhyme with "hier".

  2. Das Buch gehört ___ Lehrer. (The book belongs to the teacher.)
